summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y2–Y3, US Grade 2): partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares, then find the total using rows × columns rather than counting one by one. The equal-unit tiling (no gaps or overlaps) makes the count structural, formalises the array, and builds the bridge to area-by-counting-squares (CCSS 2.G.2 feeding 3.MD.7 and 3.OA; UK Y2–Y3 array work underpinning Y4 area). The central insight is that a tiled rectangle IS an array and its total comes from its structure.
misconceptions: Partitioning into unequal squares/pieces (not same-size units).
Leaving gaps or overlapping squares when tiling.
Counting every square one-by-one instead of using rows × columns.
Confusing the number of rows with the number of squares in a row.
Not connecting the grid count to a multiplication fact (treating it as pure counting).

activities.title: Build and read a tiled rectangle grid
steps: Set the number of rows and the number of columns for a rectangle, and watch it fill with same-size squares that snap to a grid; if a partition leaves gaps or overlaps, notice it flagged and correct it so the squares are equal and aligned.
First count the squares one-by-one (slowly), then switch to a rows × columns view and watch the same rectangle resolve to its total instantly — e.g. 4 rows of 6 squares becoming 4×6 = 24.
Write the multiplication fact that matches the grid you built, and say how many squares are in each row and how many rows there are.
Add one more column (or one more row) and predict the new total before revealing it.
activities.insight: A rectangle tiled with equal squares is a rectangular array; its total comes from rows × columns, not from counting each square, and this square-count is what area will later measure.

activities.title: Partition on paper and count by structure (performance task)
steps: On a given rectangle whose width is 4/3 of its height (e.g. 8 cm wide by 6 cm tall), mark ticks the same distance apart (e.g. every 2 cm) along a long side and a short side, then rule lines through them to divide it into 3 rows and 4 columns of equal-sized squares.
Find the total number of squares and say aloud how you counted — one by one, by repeated addition (4 + 4 + 4), by skip-counting (4, 8, 12), or as 3 × 4.
State which multiplication fact matches your grid.
activities.insight: Creating equal, aligned squares and then using the row/column structure to count — rather than drawing any lines and tallying singly — is what shows a secure grasp of the array that underlies area.

activities.title: Check the equal-unit requirement and the array link
steps: Choose the correctly-tiled rectangle from options that include a ragged or overlapping partition, and say why the equal-size, gap-free one is correct.
Give the total for a shown grid by completing rows × columns = ?.
Match a shown grid to its matching multiplication fact.
activities.insight: Equal-size squares that tile with no gaps or overlaps are what make the count structural; the grid's total is the product of its rows and columns.

checkQuestion: Here is a rectangle. Divide it into 3 rows and 4 columns of equal-sized squares, then find the total number of squares — and tell me how you counted them. (Watch whether the squares are equal-sized and gap-free, whether rows and columns align, and whether they count by ones or by rows.)
checkAnswer: A tidy 3-by-4 grid of 12 equal squares, counted efficiently as 4 + 4 + 4 or 4, 8, 12 (or 3 × 4) rather than one-by-one — relating the rows-and-columns to a rectangular array.
